topic.name: The First Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms

question.text: Given that \begin{align*} \mathcal L\left\{t^n\right\} &= \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}, && s > 0, \end{align*} use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = 5t + 3t^2e^{3t}$ for $s > 3.$
question.explanation:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

\begin{align*} \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} &= \mathcal{L}\left\{ 5t + 3t^2e^{3t} \right\} \\[5pt] &= \mathcal{L}\left\{ 5t \right\} + \mathcal{L}\left\{ 3t^2e^{3t} \right\} \\[5pt] &= 5\mathcal{L}\left\{ t \right\} + 3\mathcal{L}\left\{ t^2e^{3t} \right\} \end{align*}

We are given that, for $s > 0,$ \begin{align*} \mathcal L\left\{t^n\right\} &= \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have the following: \begin{align} \mathcal{L}\left\{ t \right\} &= \dfrac{1}{s^2} \\[5pt] \mathcal{L}\left\{ t^2 \right\} &= \dfrac{2}{s^3} \end{align}

The first shifting theorem states that if $\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$ then $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).$ Therefore, \[ \mathcal{L}\left\{ t^2e^{3t} \right\} = \dfrac{2}{(s-3)^3}. \]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

\begin{align} \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} &= 5\mathcal{L}\left\{ t \right\} + 3\mathcal{L}\left\{ t^2e^{3t} \right\} \\[5pt] &= 5 \cdot \dfrac{1}{s^2} + 3 \cdot \dfrac{2}{(s-3)^3}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{s^2} + \dfrac{6}{(s-3)^3} . \end{align}

This transform is valid for $s>3.$

example.title: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity

question.text: Consider a function $y(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{y(t)\} = Y(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{4t} y(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
question.explanation:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

\begin{align} \mathcal{L}\{e^{4t} y(t)\} &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-st} \cdot e^{4t} \, y(t)} \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-(s-4)t}} \, y(t)\, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] \end{align}

Now, recall that $\displaystyle Y(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, y(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, \[ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-4)t} \, y(t)\, \textrm{d}t = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{Y(s−4)}, \] where \[ s - 4 > s_0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{s > s_0 +4}. \]

question.text: Consider a function $q(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{q(t)\} = Q(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{9t} q(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
question.explanation:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

\begin{align} \mathcal{L}\{e^{9t} q(t)\} &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-st} \cdot e^{9t} \, q(t)} \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-(s-9)t}} \, q(t)\, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] \end{align}

Now, recall that $\displaystyle Q(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, q(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, \[ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-9)t} \, q(t)\, \textrm{d}t = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{Q(s−9)}, \] where \[ s - 9 > s_0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{s > s_0 +9}. \]

question.text: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{f(t)\} = F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-2t} f(t)\}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
question.choice1: Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $2$ units to the left.
question.choice2: Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $2$ units to the right.
question.choice3: Scale the graph of $F(s)$ by a scale factor of $2$ horizontally.
question.choice4: Scale the graph of $F(s)$ by a scale factor of $2$ vertically.
question.explanation:
The first shifting theorem states that if $ \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s), $ then $ \mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a). $

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by $e^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

  • If $a > 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

  • If $a < 0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-2t} f(t)\},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $2$ units to the left.
